doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: The business of music today: self-booking and open audiences
summary: Booking and driving take time from practice; agents underestimate audiences.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: transportation, food and budgets and everything. So it takes up so much time that you have to, it’s difficult to get the amount of hours needed to be very very proficient on your instrument, the way I like to be. So I admit that I am slipping a bit right now, but that’s because it’s just the business of music is overwhelming. Because most musicians right now book themselves. I’m driving the van. You transport yourself and everything. It’s like another thing about self-determination. You want the music to thrive and everything. If you don’t do it, who’s going to do it. So you have to begin to just do it and everything. And what most musicians are finding out — because if I tell an agent that, if I send him a CD of what I play and then I say I want to book a gig in Utica, New York, he’ll say, “Nobody in Utica, New York wants to hear what you are playing.” I mean because you heard it, it was very very progressive and everything. So they think there’d be no one in Utica that would want to hear anything like that you know. So what musicians are starting to find out is that audiences are a lot more sophisticated than a lot of agents are giving them credit for you know. They’re very very sophisticated and they’re very open to all kinds of music, all kinds of styles you know.
